cases.query: Every generating family reconstructs x by the same unique coordinate formula.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℚ, the generating family (1,1) has representations 1=1·1+0·1=0·1+1·1. Independence is essential for unique coordinates.

cases.query: Two distinct coefficient vectors on a basis can give the same vector.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For any basis, subtracting the combinations gives a linear dependence; all coefficient differences are zero, so the claimed distinctness is impossible.

cases.query: Any prescription on an arbitrary spanning family extends to a linear map.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In ℚ, prescribe the images of the repeated spanning family (1,1) to be (0,1). A function cannot send 1 to both values.

cases.query: A linear map applies f to each coefficient rather than preserving coefficients in a basis expansion.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: The coefficients lie in K, whereas f has domain V. For f:ℚ²→ℚ the proposed f(aᵢ) is not even typed; the correct formula applies f to basis vectors.

cases.query: The image of a map is only the set of its basis images.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For identity on ℚ² the basis image set is {e₁,e₂}, but e₁+e₂ is also in the range. The span, not the finite set, is required.

cases.query: Every map prescribed on a basis is injective.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Choose every prescribed image to be zero on a nonzero source. The constructed map is zero and sends every pair to the same value.

cases.query: Independent prescribed images always make a map surjective.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: The map ℚ→ℚ² with prescribed image e₁ is injective, but e₂ is not in its range. The images must span the target.

cases.query: Agreement on one nonzero vector always determines a linear map.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: On ℚ², identity and projection onto the first coordinate agree on e₁ but differ on e₂. Agreement is needed on a spanning family.

cases.query: Multiplication by the representing matrix gives the output vector in the original abstract space.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: A matrix acts on coordinate functions, not on an arbitrary carrier V. For an abstract target W the output must first be expressed in its selected basis.

cases.query: A linear map has the same matrix in all bases.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: On ℚ² take f=diag(1,2) in the standard basis. Swapping the basis gives diag(2,1), so uniqueness requires fixed source and target bases.

cases.query: The matrix of g∘f is M(f)M(g) in unreversed order.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For f=[[1,1],[0,1]] and g=diag(2,1), gf has upper-right entry 2 while fg has upper-right entry 1. The order is M(g)M(f).

cases.query: Matrix representation sends a sum of maps to the product of their matrices.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: On ℚ, maps f=g=identity have sum matrix [2], whereas the product of their matrices is [1].

cases.query: b.toMatrix c converts b-coordinates into c-coordinates.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: On ℚ let b=(1), c=(2), x=2. b.toMatrix c=[2]. Multiplying b-coordinate 2 gives 4, but the c-coordinate is 1. It converts c-coordinates to b-coordinates.

cases.query: One may reverse the order of successive coordinate changes.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: In dimension two, choose successive transition matrices [[1,1],[0,1]] and diag(2,1). They do not commute: upper-right entries of the products are 1 and 2.

cases.query: Every coordinate-change matrix is its own inverse.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: On ℚ with b=(1), c=(2), the change is [2] and the reverse change [1/2], which are unequal.

cases.query: Changing source and target bases always uses one conjugating matrix.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For a map ℚ→ℚ² the representing matrix is 2×1. Its source and target changes have sizes 1×1 and 2×2, so a single conjugation is not defined.

cases.query: An eigenvector list, even dependent, gives a diagonal matrix representation.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For a nonzero square-zero Jordan block on ℚ², its only eigenvectors lie on the first coordinate line. Repeating e₁ gives eigenvectors but no basis, and the operator is not diagonalizable.

cases.query: Every linear functional equals the sum of the coordinate functionals without coefficients.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: On ℚ take standard basis and φ(x)=2x. Its coordinate functional is x↦x; coefficient φ(1)=2 is necessary.

cases.query: Coordinate functionals corresponding to a redundant spanning family remain independent.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: A redundant list is not a basis and does not provide a unique coordinate map. On ℚ the repeated list (1,1) cannot yield two independent functionals in the one-dimensional dual.

cases.query: Every subgroup of an abelian group has a direct-sum complement.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: The subgroup 2ℤ of ℤ has no complement: every nonzero subgroup intersects it nontrivially, while the zero subgroup does not span ℤ with 2ℤ. The field/vector-space hypotheses matter.

cases.query: Every injective homomorphism of modules over any ring has a left inverse.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Multiplication by 2 on the ℤ-module ℤ is injective. A ℤ-linear left inverse would send 2 to 1, impossible because its value on 2 is twice its value on 1.

cases.query: Every surjective homomorphism of modules over any ring has a right inverse.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: The quotient ℤ→ℤ/2ℤ is surjective, but a section would give a nonzero element of order two in ℤ. Splitting here relies on vector spaces over a field.

cases.query: P(f)x=P(z)x for every x without an eigenvector hypothesis.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Let f=diag(1,2), x=e₁+e₂, z=1, P=X over ℚ. Then f(x)=e₁+2e₂ differs from z x.

cases.query: Every characteristic root exists in the base field.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: The real rotation matrix [[0,-1],[1,0]] has characteristic polynomial X²+1, with no real root. The equivalence concerns a supplied scalar z in K.

cases.query: A root of an arbitrary polynomial implies it is an eigenvalue of f.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Take f=identity on ℚ and P=X. The polynomial has root 0, but 0 is not an eigenvalue of identity. Minimality/annihilation conditions cannot be omitted.

cases.query: The characteristic polynomial always divides the minimal polynomial.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For identity on ℚ², χ=(X-1)² but the minimal polynomial is X-1. The divisibility direction is the reverse.

cases.query: P(f)=0 iff P divides the minimal polynomial.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For f=identity on ℚ, P=(X-1)² annihilates f, but does not divide minpoly(f)=X-1. The minimal polynomial divides P.

cases.query: Commuting maps send every eigenvector to a nonzero eigenvector.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Take f=identity, g=zero. They commute, but g sends every nonzero vector to zero. Eigenspace membership includes zero; being an eigenvector does not.

cases.query: Commuting maps over any field must have a common eigenbasis.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: A nonzero square-zero map commutes with identity, but the square-zero map has no eigenbasis. Commutation alone does not imply diagonalizability.

cases.query: Every scalar is an eigenvalue of an operator diagonal in a basis.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Identity on ℚ has diagonal entry 1 only; scalar 2 is not an eigenvalue. Eigenvalues must occur among the actual diagonal entries.

cases.query: The set-theoretic union of eigenspaces of a diagonal operator is the entire space.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For diag(1,2) on ℚ², eigenspaces are the coordinate axes and {0}; e₁+e₂ lies in neither axis. Their subspace supremum is the whole space, not their set union.

cases.query: Adding t times a row to itself always preserves the determinant.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For A=[1] over ℚ and t=1 the updated matrix is [2]. The distinct-row hypothesis is necessary.

cases.query: Scaling one row by t multiplies determinant by t raised to n.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For A=I₂ over ℚ and t=2, scaling only the first row yields determinant 2, not 4. The exponent n applies when every row is scaled.

cases.query: Right multiplication by Eᵢⱼ(t) performs the same row addition as left multiplication.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: With A=diag(2,3), i=1,j=2,t=1, EA has upper-right entry 3 but AE has upper-right entry 2. Right multiplication performs a column operation.

cases.query: Eᵢᵢ(-t) is always inverse to Eᵢᵢ(t).
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: Over ℚ take t=1. Eᵢᵢ(1) scales the selected coordinate by 2, while Eᵢᵢ(-1) kills it; their product is not identity.

cases.query: Row operations may be applied to the coefficient matrix without changing the right hand side.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For A=I₂, y=e₂, add row 2 to row 1. Original x=e₂ solves Ax=y, but transformed A times e₂ is e₁+e₂, not y. The right hand side must also be transformed.

cases.query: A nonzero diagonal matrix unit can also be square zero.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: For arbitrary nonzero t in a field, (tEᵢᵢ)²=t²Eᵢᵢ≠0. The distinct-index hypothesis makes the off-diagonal matrix unit square to zero.

cases.query: Eᵢⱼ(t) is never identity, even when t=0.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: With t=0 the transvection is exactly identity. Nonzero coefficient is required for the nonidentity conclusion.

cases.query: Every square-zero map has no eigenbasis, including the zero map.
cases.counterexample_or_missing_premise: The zero endomorphism is diagonal on every basis with all eigenvalues zero. The nonzero-map hypothesis is essential.
